cards.title: What one word can't hold
cards.body: Several of today's pieces circle the same problem: the instruments we use to register experience are cruder than the experience. Arabic keeps four words for sadness where English keeps one; Bergson argues most of what you see is memory filling in the gaps; Jim Nielsen notes you already know the thumbs-up misrepresents you, right up until you're the one reading the data. Start with the four sadnesses — it's the rare piece that hands you working vocabulary, and you'll feel the gap it names the next time someone asks how you're doing. cards.title: Arabic has four sadnesses. Your therapist hears one.
cards.body: Huzn is grief pointed backwards, at a loss already suffered. Ghamm is a present weight that covers the heart like a cloud; ka'aba is dejection deep enough to show in the face. A researcher running sentiment analysis on 25,025 Arabic comments about trauma watched all of them collapse into a single label: sadness.
cards.predict: Guess first: what separates huzn from ordinary sadness — its intensity, or its direction in time?

sections.text:
Turn an ordinary complaint about a bad week into a question about what suffering is for, and someone in the room will call you mufalsaf — or mufalsafah, if you're a woman. It is affectionate teasing, built from falsafah, philosophy. Ma titfalsafi: don't philosophise. Ya faylasuf: oh, look, a philosopher.

Chereen Shurafa, a psychotherapist turned researcher at Hamad bin Khalifa University in Qatar, thinks the joke carries a cost. Buried in it is the assumption that philosophical thought sits outside daily life — and nowhere does that assumption do more damage than in conversations about mental health.

Her day job is computational. She runs sentiment analysis, which sorts text into positive, negative or neutral, and emotion annotation, which sorts it into categories like sadness, fear and anger, starting with her reading and labelling entries by hand. She has applied both to tens of thousands of Arabic social media comments on trauma, loneliness during COVID-19, and gendered narratives of depression. For one recent project she assembled a corpus of more than 170,000 YouTube comments on trauma videos and worked through 25,025 of them.

The methods genuinely work. They surface patterns across hundreds of thousands of comments, catch shifts in tone over time, return results instantly. But the more Arabic she fed them, the more she noticed what fell out the bottom.

Take diq alsadr, a phrase that comes out of the Quran. Rendered into English it becomes a tightness or narrowing of the chest and stops there — a body complaint. In Arabic the chest is the seat of consciousness and spiritual receptivity, and the narrowing is a condition of the whole inner person, not a symptom below the collarbone. A clinician who hears it as anxiety with somatic features will reach for tools that relieve the sensation and never touch the meaning.

Then there is the sadness vocabulary, which the classifier flattens into one bucket. Huzn appears in the Quran, is carried by the prophets, and runs through classical poetry as a mark of spiritual depth rather than weakness — and it points backwards, at a loss that has already happened. Ghamm is now: an overwhelming, suffocating weight that covers the heart like a cloud. Ka'aba is heavier and longer, a dejection that becomes visible in the face and the body, which the medieval scholar Ibn al-Qayyim was careful to distinguish from both of the others. Asaf is sorrow shot through with regret.

These are not four shades of one feeling. Each names a different relationship to suffering, and choosing between them is an act of precision — "This is the exact form of what I'm holding." Reduce that to a facile label and what you lose is clinical understanding.

Shurafa's proposal is that the frameworks for reading such precision already exist and are simply going unused. Classical Islamic psychology — Ibn Sina, Al-Ghazali, Ibn al-Qayyim — treated mental health as the psychological, emotional and spiritual wellbeing of one whole person.

Her example is al-Kindi, born in Kufa around 801 CE, educated in Baghdad, later titled the Philosopher of the Arabs. In The Epistle on the Device for Dispelling Sorrows he defines sorrow as pain of the soul, arriving when we lose something we love or fail to obtain something we desire. If you want something that cannot possibly exist, you will never have it; and since everything material is transitory, believing that anything will last guarantees endless suffering. His remedy is not to kill desire but to train good habits until they become second nature, and to move your attachments off what perishes onto what endures — an internal adjustment, rather than an attempt to fix a world that will not hold still.

That is recognisably a cognitive technique, arriving a thousand years early. The difference, Shurafa argues, is that al-Kindi never separated psychological health from questions of meaning, virtue and flourishing, which makes his frame wider than most CBT rather than more primitive than it.

She is careful about what she is not saying. Not abandoning evidence-based treatment or contemporary neuroscience. Not returning to the 11th century and applying it whole — those frameworks are to be built on, not restored. And simplification, she grants, is sometimes necessary in psychology as in philosophy. What she wants is epistemological pluralism: a therapist in Qatar or Lebanon or Iraq reaching for contemporary protocols and classical frameworks both, a researcher running the classifier and then reading its output with philosophy at her elbow.

Which turns the joke inside out. Being mufalsafah, in her account, is not overthinking. It is "thinking with sufficient care" — care enough to leave the distinctions in.

sections.label: Steelman
sections.text: The reductive tools earn their keep in exactly the way the essay concedes: they move across hundreds of thousands of comments, track tone over time, and answer immediately, which no amount of philological care can do at that scale. And the case for the finer vocabulary is argued on grounds of meaning and clinical understanding rather than demonstrated on outcomes — nothing here shows a patient who got better because someone parsed huzn correctly rather than ghamm.

sections.label: Key takeaways
items: Huzn points backwards at a loss already suffered; ghamm is a present, suffocating weight over the heart; ka'aba is prolonged dejection that shows in the face and body. Ibn al-Qayyim treated them as distinct conditions, not intensities of one.

Diq alsadr, from the Quran, names a narrowing of the whole inner person, with the chest as the seat of consciousness. Heard as anxiety with somatic features, the treatment relieves the sensation and skips the meaning.

Al-Kindi, born around 801 CE, defined sorrow as pain of the soul caused by wanting what cannot last, and prescribed habit training plus redirected attachment — CBT's move, but never severed from virtue and meaning.
The ask is epistemological pluralism, not replacement: run the sentiment classifier, then read its output with the philosophical history of the words in hand.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Naming the exact form of what you're holding isn't pedantry — it's the difference between treating a sensation and treating a loss.

recall.q: In Arabic, how do huzn, ghamm and ka'aba differ from one another?
recall.a: Huzn is oriented toward the past, toward a loss already suffered, and carries connotations of spiritual depth. Ghamm is felt in the present — a suffocating weight covering the heart. Ka'aba is deeper and more prolonged, visible in the face and body; Ibn al-Qayyim treated it as distinct from both.

cards.title: Slop isn't em dashes. It's thinness.
cards.body: Great art unfurls the more attention you give it, and the price of rewarding careful readers is repelling casual ones. That property — thickness — is also the real line between substance and AI slop, which holds no secrets and evaporates under scrutiny. Exhibit A: the sheet music painted on a naked man's backside in Bosch's hell panel, which turns out to be unplayable on purpose.
cards.predict: Guess before reading: that song painted on a man's backside in Bosch's hell panel — what happens when someone actually tries to play it?

sections.text:
In the hell panel of Hieronymus Bosch's Garden of Earthly Delights, a naked man lies pinned under a giant lute with a line of musical notation printed across his backside. A companion points at it, helpfully, as though breaking the news.

In 2012 a student at Oklahoma Christian University named Amelia Hamrick transcribed the notes, recorded them, and posted the result to her blog, which made her briefly famous worldwide. It is the perfect fun fact: five hundred years ago a painter hid a real song on a man's rear end.

Except the correction is better than the fact. Ian Pittman, who knows medieval music, laid out the problems across three blog posts. Hamrick wasn't first — a Swedish group recorded a version in 2003, Atrium Musicae did it in 1978 on an LP called Codex Gluteo, and reportedly some art historians got there in 1981 and 1961. Worse, the notation isn't music: no clef, notes spaced at random, one staff with the wrong number of lines. Every recording is therefore an invention — the same move we would call hallucination if a language model made it.

And Bosch meant it that way. Across his work, secular music is a one-way ticket to hell — church music was fine, so long as it glorified God rather than the players — which is why his musicians are being tortured: one trapped inside a drum being beaten by a demon, one crucified on a harp, and our man crushed beneath his lute. The notation isn't an easter egg. It's a warning label.

That is the essay's subject: thickness. Thick art unfurls in response to attention — the more time you give it, the more it gives back. The author spent school convinced that great literature was a hoax inflicted on adolescents, and he blames the teaching, because the works were handed to him as if everything good about them were visible from outside. They are closer to dark caves with treasure stashed inside. Nobody told him to bring a flashlight; entering the cave was 30 per cent of the grade.

The catch is built in: rewarding the careful reader usually means repelling the casual one.

He proposes four thickening agents. Roads not taken — thick work carries the marks of attempts discarded, a scrap pile larger than the finished thing. Hokusai drew the same idea at 33, at 44, at 46 and at 72, and only the last is the one you would recognise. An egg left out of the mix — Betty Crocker could include the egg powder and doesn't, because cracking an egg lets you feel you baked something, and thick art leaves an equivalent gap for you to fill. His example is the children's book The 11th Hour: you page through pretty animals playing board games, and only at the end learn a crime has been unfolding in the illustrations the whole time. The real book is the second read.

Third, reasons why. Thin art has no answer to why this word, this scene, this character; thick art does. Hamlet is full of ears — poison poured into one, characters forever eavesdropping, ears buried in the metaphors, "the whole ear of Denmark". He concedes it may be accidental and mostly unnoticed, and argues the recurrence creates a depth you feel whether or not you can name it. Fourth, blood sacrifice: cost buys thickness because human time is finite. The carved wooden altarpieces at the Met Cloisters seize you because some part of the mind estimates the hours and flags it as important — you are seeing the expenditure of a life. When Penn and Teller performed live, Penn explained before swallowing fire that it is not a trick: fire-eaters get burns, swallow fuel, inhale hydrocarbons, catch something called fire-eater's pneumonia. He asked the audience not to wonder how they did it, but why.

The absence is easier to spot. Bike mechanics joke about bicycle-shaped objects — a mass-produced thing with a seat, pedals, wheels and handlebars that still isn't a bike — and there are book-shaped and movie-shaped and thought-shaped objects too.

His specimen is a self-help passage assuring readers they are built to perform under pressure, citing research that merely reminding someone their performance improves under pressure improves it by 33 per cent. He went and read the paper. The 33 per cent isn't in it; the underlying studies are mostly about multiple-choice tests; and what participants were actually told was not that pressure improves performance but that feeling anxious doesn't necessarily mean you'll do worse. There is also evidence of publication bias for the effect. Touch any sentence and the village tips over.

The fix, though, isn't more detail. Thickness comes from surfacing a few facts so well that you sense the universe of facts behind them. Jane Jacobs demolishes planners who assume city people crave emptiness and quiet by walking you down upper Broadway, where benches sit behind concrete buffers and fill block after block with people watching pedestrians, watching traffic, watching each other — then up to the calmer, more orderly streets near Columbia, where the benches sit empty and, she reports after trying them, nothing could be more boring. The author lived on those blocks, privately called it the dead zone of Manhattan, and never worked out why. He adds that nobody really knows what drive bench-watching satisfies.

The risk in all this is obvious: praise hidden depths and you empower snobs. He thinks the pendulum swung the other way and stuck. Poptimism won, the line between thick and thin was erased, and we were left without vocabulary at the exact moment the slop arrived — which is why the working definition of slop has collapsed into em dashes, bullet points and line breaks. The real distinction is thickness. Slop holds no secrets and evaporates under scrutiny; what it offers instead is bottomlessness, infinite channels with nothing on.

So he isn't rattled by studies finding people prefer AI art to human art. Snap judgments favour thinness: pretty flowers, poems that rhyme, the simulacrum of thought. The question that matters is which things survive, which ones people cross the world to stand in front of. That is also his belated answer to why school made him read old books — age is the only quality test we can actually run. We stopped brewing Bronze Age beer and sailing Bronze Age ships, but we still tell Bronze Age stories.

The evidence is lying around already. Everyone Ghibli-fied their camera roll a few months ago and then quietly stopped, leaving millions of images in a data centre while people go on watching the actual films; on the Suno subreddit the running joke is that nobody can stand anyone else's AI music, only their own. Meanwhile his inbox fills with pitches like the one built for credible thinkers who have "a book's worth of ideas" but not the time to write one. There is no such thing. The ideas are not already good and merely awaiting the right words — they are not yet thick, and the part you'd want to automate is the only part that was ever the work.

sections.label: Steelman
sections.text: Thickness is hard to falsify, and the essay half-admits it: the ears in Hamlet may be accidental and unnoticed, which makes the depth something the reader supplies rather than something the work contains. Any piece you love can be credited with hidden riches and any piece you don't dismissed as a book-shaped object. And survival-as-proof mostly rewards whatever institutions kept copying and teaching — the very canon-making he once suspected was a racket.

sections.label: Key takeaways
items: Thickness is responsiveness: the more attention you give a work, the more it returns. The built-in cost is that what rewards the careful reader tends to repel the casual one.

Bosch's notation has no clef, randomly spaced notes and a staff with the wrong number of lines, so every recorded version of the butt music is invented. He painted it unplayable because he thought secular music damned you — it's a warning, not an easter egg.
Thick art leaves you an egg to crack. In The 11th Hour the crime hides in illustrations you've already flipped past, so the actual reading experience is the reread.
Slop is not a punctuation style, it's thinness — work that holds no secrets. The tell: Ghibli-fied camera rolls sit unopened in a data centre while people keep watching the films.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Ask of anything: why did they do it, and what did it cost them? Thin work has no answer.

recall.q: What is 'thickness' in art, what four things produce it, and what's the tell for its absence?
recall.a: Thickness is art that unfurls in response to attention. Four agents: roads not taken (Hokusai reworking one idea at 33, 44, 46, 72), an egg left for you to crack (The 11th Hour's hidden crime), internal reasons why (ears recurring throughout Hamlet), and blood sacrifice (Penn eating real fire — ask why, not how). Thinness holds no secrets and evaporates under scrutiny; that, not em dashes, is what slop is.

cards.title: Fetch the answer before the key comes back up
cards.body: Wirewiki fires its autocomplete request on keyDown and renders on keyUp, buying roughly 121 ms of budget — enough that results are usually waiting before your finger lifts. Behind it, 240 million domain names sit in a trie plus a memory-mapped block index that answers in about 2 ms. The bottleneck turned out to be geography, not code.

sections.text:
Type into most search boxes and you can feel the wait. It's small, but it's there, because the request only leaves after the keystroke is finished — every millisecond of network becomes a millisecond of dead air.

Wirewiki is a site for inspecting internet infrastructure: DNS records, delegation, mail deliverability config. There are dozens of tools like it, so its author picked UX as the way to stand out, and since autocomplete is how you navigate the site, the target became next-frame instant.

The move is to shift the request earlier inside the keystroke. On keyDown — the moment the key goes down, before it comes back up — the client fetches suggestions. On keyUp it renders. Type w-i-k: the request for wi fires the instant the i is pressed, and if the response lands before the k is released, completions for wik are already sitting there. The budget is the first press, plus the gap, plus the second press. Measured across 100 domain names typed at a decent clip, that's 121 ms at p99. A 60 Hz frame is 16.7 ms, which is the slack you're actually racing.

The response carries not just the current prefix but every possible next character, which sounds like it should wreck the payload. It doesn't, because domain names have only 38 legal characters: a-z, 0-9, hyphen, dot. Eight suggestions for the prefix plus eight for each next character caps the response at 312 names — about 5 kB, 2.5 kB compressed. A healthy image is 50-100 kB, so the whole fan-out costs less than a picture nobody thinks twice about.

Underneath sit two structures split by popularity. The head is the Tranco top million, held in an in-memory trie with the top 8 suggestions precomputed at every prefix, so a lookup is a walk of a few pointers. The tail is everything else: 240 million gTLD names from CZDS, sorted, delta-compressed into fixed blocks, memory-mapped off SSD at about 2.5 GB. A query binary-searches a 27 MB in-memory directory, then linearly scans a single 256-name block, with hot pages held by the OS page cache. Both the corpus and the query length are bounded, so the worst case is effectively constant.

Under a stress test of 720,000 keystroke queries replayed open-loop — fired at a fixed rate regardless of whether responses came back — most requests were answered by the API in 2 ms, and nginx plus API stayed inside 15 ms at p99 even at 1,600 requests per second.

Which is where the honest part starts, because none of that is the constraint. End-to-end latency works out to the browser-through-Cloudflare-to-server round trip plus about 10 ms, and the server is one box in Europe. From the US, add 100-200 ms and the p99 claim dies — hence the asterisk in the title. Shaving further milliseconds off a 2 ms API buys nothing. The only fix left is geographic, and the author decided multiple servers with geo load balancing was more than a niche tool deserved.

sections.label: Do this
items: Move the fetch to keyDown rather than keyUp or a debounce timer. You gain the full press duration plus the inter-key gap without issuing a single extra request.
Measure your own typing budget before optimizing anything: log press-to-next-release times over real input and take the p99. Here it was a concrete 121 ms, not a guess.
Check whether prefetching every next state is actually expensive. When the alphabet is small and bounded, the entire fan-out can weigh less than one image on the page.
Profile the whole path before tuning the hot loop. If your handler answers in 2 ms and the CDN round trip is 80, the next win is a point of presence, not a better data structure.

sections.label: When not to
sections.text: The asterisk is doing real work: the target only holds near the server. Traffic from the US misses at p99, and the remedy is geographic distribution rather than code — which the author judged excessive for a side project, leaning on CDN caching of hot paths and Nielsen's 0.1 s instantaneous threshold to cover the gap. Past 2 ms, more API optimization is wasted effort the network eats anyway.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The fastest request is the one you sent before the user finished asking.

recall.q: How do you make autocomplete results ready before the user finishes the keystroke?
recall.a: Fire the request on keyDown instead of keyUp and prefetch suggestions for every possible next character. That buys the press duration plus the inter-key gap — about 121 ms at p99 for fast typing — and with only 38 legal domain characters the whole fan-out is ~312 names, roughly 2.5 kB compressed.

cards.title: Singapore fixed its water. Food is a harder bet.
cards.body: In 2019 The Economist's index ranked Singapore the most food-secure country on earth — and that same year Singapore launched a plan to grow 30 per cent of its own food by 2030 on under 1 per cent of its land. Five years on, eggs are up six percentage points and vegetables and seafood are down. Its water program, built against a threat someone actually made out loud, went the other way.
cards.predict: Singapore vowed in 2019 to grow 30 per cent of its food locally by 2030. Guess which direction its local vegetable production had moved by 2024.

sections.text:
In May 2010 the historian Peter Coclanis was in Brunei, invited to give two lectures on agriculture. The sultanate had just announced a push to grow its own rice — food security, self-sufficiency, the whole vocabulary. Afterwards a journalist asked the visiting expert what he made of the plan, and he said, on the record, in the country that had flown him in, that it was wrongheaded.

His reasoning was blunt. Brunei is a tiny, gas-and-oil-rich sultanate of tropical rainforest on ecologically fragile Borneo, sitting inside the region that grows more rice than any other on the planet. Carry on with carbon and buy the rice. Fifteen years of assiduous effort later, Brunei grew 8 per cent of the rice it ate in 2024, up from 4.8 per cent in 2017 — and if it insists on the goal, Coclanis argues, it would do better to lease farmland abroad and hire people to grow rice properly than to grow it badly on bad soil at home.

That small case is his way into a large one. Since the supply-chain shocks of COVID, governments everywhere have been buying food security and sustainability come hell or high water, and almost nobody is pricing the opportunity cost. Singapore is the most sophisticated version of the experiment, which makes it the most useful — because it splits cleanly into a triumph and a mistake.

Start with water, the triumph. Small islands run short of fresh water, and colonial Singapore did the obvious thing: MacRitchie Reservoir in 1867, Lower Peirce in 1910, Upper Seletar in 1940. From 1927 it also piped water across from the Malaysian state of Johor, an arrangement formalised in the agreements of 1961 and 1962. At independence in 1965, at least half of Singapore's fresh water arrived through someone else's territory.

That year, during the Konfrontasi with Indonesia and Malaysia, the Malaysian prime minister Tunku Abdul Rahman told the British high commissioner that if Singapore's foreign policy went against Malaysian interests, pressure could be applied by "threatening to turn off the water in Johor." Coclanis is careful that the remark was made in a hot moment and should be read in context. Singapore's leaders read it differently. They never forgot it.

What followed was half a century of unglamorous engineering and one crucial pricing decision: water was sold as a scarce and invaluable resource rather than a free good, so demand itself was shaped. On the supply side came rainwater harvesting, surface and underground drainage, dammed river estuaries, and the Marina Barrage, which converted a salty bay into a freshwater reservoir.

Then, in the 2000s, two entirely new taps. NEWater — sewage reclaimed through microfiltration, reverse osmosis and UV, and safe to drink — arrived in 2002; the first desalination plant opened in 2005. The environment minister Lim Swee Say gave the country its slogan of Four National Taps in 2004, and by 2009 Malaysian imports were down to about 40 per cent. The Johor deal runs to 2061, and the expectation is that when it lapses, roughly 85 per cent of Singapore's water will come from reclamation and desalination. Most experts now think the island's supply is secure for the rest of the century.

Now food. The 30 by 30 plan, launched in 2019, promised that 30 per cent of what Singaporeans eat would be grown in Singapore by 2030 — on less than 1 per cent of the island's land, in a country that then imported more than 90 per cent of its food.

The facts underneath that promise are strange. Agriculture, forestry and fishing rounded to 0.0 per cent of Singapore's GDP in 2024, down from 3.1 per cent in 1965 — the joint-lowest share in the world, alongside Hong Kong, Aruba and San Marino. Groceries take about 7 per cent of household income, the lowest figure anywhere outside the United States, and even adding the country's beloved hawker stalls, which UNESCO recognised in 2020, total food spending sits near 20 per cent.

Stranger still: in 2019, the very year 30 by 30 launched, the Economist Intelligence Unit ranked Singapore the most food-secure country in the world, first of 113. It fell to 28th by 2022, but mainly because the index changed what it measured, adding weight to farmer-focused criteria, the first mile from farm to market, and resiliency.

The execution was serious, because the People's Action Party is never unserious. Agribiotech, automation, vertical farming, closed-containment aquaculture, novel foods, precision nutrition research at Danone Nutricia's D-Lab in Biopolis, a new Singapore Food Agency, and an 18-hectare Agri-Food Innovation Park at Sungei Kadut announced in 2019 and now due in 2026. Singapore became a global centre for lab-grown meat by 2022; by 2024 high costs, scaling problems and consumer indifference had stalled it and killed some startups. The Food Agency approved 16 insect species for eating in 2024, and heavy regulation slowed that too.

Some things did work. Egg production automated well, aquaculture grew, and Sky Greens showed that vegetables in vertical silos are viable — just expensive, because the towers run on energy. Flowers do well vertically too; strawberries might.

The scoreboard through 2024 is one gain and two losses: hen eggs up six percentage points, vegetables and seafood each down about one. And the government's own 2024 report has quietly changed its language, boasting instead about a supply chain spanning 187 countries and regions, up from 140 two decades ago, and demoting local production from a buffer or an insurance policy to a "complement" in a multi-pronged approach.

Coclanis's objection is not that Singapore lacks the brainpower. It is that 30 per cent is an arbitrary number — why not 20, or 50? — and that resiliency has costs that are real and sometimes steep. He says he would have been more bullish if the honest goal was building agribiotech expertise rather than filling plates. On the sustainability argument he is harsher: Singapore is an entrepôt with one of the highest trade-to-GDP ratios on earth, and its entire carbon footprint is a rounding error in global accounting. Trimming food miles changes nothing.

The two halves of the island's story rhyme in a useful way. The water program worked because it was aimed at a specific vulnerability with a name, a date and a hand on a valve. The food program was aimed at a feeling that arrived with the pandemic and has been leaving ever since.

sections.label: Steelman
sections.text: The water story is itself the strongest case for the food plan. Comparative advantage holds only while ships sail and neighbours stay friendly, and Singapore learned in 1965 exactly what it feels like when a supplier mentions the valve — capacity you never build is capacity you cannot summon in a crisis. The EIU's own re-weighting toward resiliency and the first mile is a concession that import strength, however dominant, is a thinner kind of security than the rankings once implied.

sections.label: Key takeaways
items: Brunei is the control experiment: fifteen years of pushing rice self-sufficiency moved it from 4.8 per cent of consumption in 2017 to 8 per cent in 2024. The effort is real; the needle barely moves.

Singapore's water win came from two moves, not one — pricing water as scarce rather than free to shape demand, and inventing new supply (NEWater in 2002, desalination in 2005) until Malaysian imports fell from half at independence to about 40 per cent by 2009.

Through 2024, 30 by 30 delivered eggs up six percentage points and vegetables and seafood each down about one, and the 2024 government report now calls local production a complement rather than a buffer.

Singapore was ranked the world's most food-secure country in 2019 — the year it decided its food security needed fixing. Its drop to 28th by 2022 was mostly a change in scoring methodology, not in Singapore.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Before you pay for self-sufficiency, name the hand that could turn off the tap — if you cannot name one, you are insuring against a mood.

recall.q: Why does Coclanis judge Singapore's water program a success and its 30 by 30 food plan a mistake?
recall.a: Water answered a named vulnerability — Malaysia's leader once threatened to cut off Johor's supply — and Singapore engineered its way out with pricing, NEWater and desalination, aiming for 85 per cent self-supply by 2061. Food was already secure: Singapore ranked first in the world in 2019, agriculture is 0.0 per cent of GDP, and chasing an arbitrary 30 per cent on under 1 per cent of land spends against its real advantages in trade and logistics.
